Author: @thumbsup-1
Content:
I don't expect anyone to read this but I'm posting this in every video where I'm early

Usually, satellites and probes need to burn rocket fuel to propel themselves to Low or High Earth Orbit. That's already a pretty expensive burn. For example, the Falcon 9  needs to burn approximately 900 000 gallons of fuel and oxidiser to get to Low Earth orbit. However, if you want to go higher or farther than that, let's say High Earth Orbit or interplanetary missions, you need a third stage. Specifically, a Centaur stage. That stage also uses a significant amount of fuel to get the amount of Delta Vee needed to get to the destination. And I think that's unnecessary, especially for smaller probes like CubeSats. That's where my idea comes into play. 


On Earth, a company called SpinLaunch is using a 45 meter spinning arm that spins at 450 RPM with the payload at the end, and lets go of it at the right time to basically ‘throw’ satellites into space, which reduces launch costs by a lot. And that, I think, is quite clever. The part that isn't so clever is that they're doing this on Earth, Where there's an atmosphere. So, they need to create a special launching machine that needs the air inside of it vacuumed out enough so that the payload they're launching doesn't burn up. This also makes it easier to launch it at high speeds with less air resistance. But in space, you have an even better vacuum and you have way more space to spin a longer tether or arm, and thus launch satellites at way higher speeds. 


To take advantage of this, we can first launch a big cubical satellite, (let's name that A) that’s connected by a tether to a payload that weighs about 50 kg, ( let's name that B) and a counterweight the same weight as the payload, (let's name that C), on opposite sides of A. the counterweight is launched at the same time as the payload to minimise recoil on A. They're both attached to A on opposite sides by a 1000 meter long 2 cm thick Zylon rope. They're coiled up in a spool to minimize space taken. From there, they can be launched to Low earth orbit or high earth orbit. And I know this part needs fuel, but come on. I'm talking about travelling through space, not the atmosphere. 


Once they're in space, ‘A’ starts spinning using a steel reaction wheel. It first spins to 30 RPM, then 70, 100, 150, then 200. Once it reaches 300 RPM, the spool holding the tether will be unlocked. The tether (not the payload) will be pulled out by the centrifugal force. Then, the payload will slowly ride up the tether and once it reaches the tip, the tether will be cut. 

 To prevent B from being damaged because of the G force acting on it, we can epoxy pot the components. This is basically pouring a really thick glue into the satellite and letting it harden to create a thick, rubbery coating around the components.. Because of this, all of the components are locked in place and don't move, which thus helps the parts survive.


Using explosive bolts and a precise radio signal trigger, the tether is cut from A. This is the final stage. After this, Payload B,  just by spinning alone, will be travelling at about 94000 meters per second. But sadly there G force will thanks snap the payload
